# Function to extract a value out of the contrast figures by species and contrast
fig.val.fcn <- function(dat, spp.x, cont, rnd){
dat.source <- if(dat == "g") grow.diff else mort.diff
k <- if(dat == "g") 1 else 2
IvS2 <- cm2.fcn(k, results.table = dat.source$IvS2)
I_LMH2 <- cm2.fcn(k, results.table = dat.source$I_LMH2)
S_LMH2 <- cm2.fcn(k, results.table = dat.source$S_LMH2)
tab.comb <- bind_rows(IvS2, I_LMH2, S_LMH2)

val.out <- round(tab.comb$Means[tab.comb$Species == spp.x & tab.comb$Domain == cont], rnd)
return(val.out)
}


# Significant findings, Growth

grow.n.I <- nrow(grow.diff$I_LMH2)
grow.n.S <- nrow(grow.diff$S_LMH2)

grow.IvS.sig <- length(grow.diff$IvS2$significant[grow.diff$IvS2$significant == TRUE])
grow.IvS.signeg <- length(grow.diff$IvS2$significant[grow.diff$IvS2$significant == TRUE & grow.diff$IvS2$Means < 0])
grow.I.sig <- length(grow.diff$I_LMH2$significant[grow.diff$I_LMH2$significant == TRUE])
grow.I.signeg <- length(grow.diff$I_LMH2$significant[grow.diff$I_LMH2$significant == TRUE & grow.diff$I_LMH2$Means < 0])
grow.S.sig <- length(grow.diff$S_LMH2$significant[grow.diff$S_LMH2$significant == TRUE])
grow.S.signeg <- length(grow.diff$S_LMH2$significant[grow.diff$S_LMH2$significant == TRUE & grow.diff$S_LMH2$Means < 0])

# CWD amounts, tapping values from the initial & delta CWD tables in the suppliment
init.cwd.stats <- analysis.stats$init.cwd.stats %>%
  mutate(range05.95 = q95 - q05) %>%

cwd.summ.fcn <- function(data.2use, col.interest, place, stat.use) {
end.start <- switch(stat.use, "min" = 1, "max" = n.spp) # Which row end (top or bottom) to start on?
place2 <- if(stat.use == "min") place else n.spp - place + 1

x <- data.2use %>% arrange(get(col.interest))
x2 <- x[place2, ]
x2.range <- paste0("(5th percentile = ", x2$q05, " mm, 95th percentile = ", x2$q95, " mm)")
x2.range.full <- paste0("(5th-95th percentile range = ", x2$range05.95, " mm, 5th percentile = ", x2$q05, " mm, 95th percentile = ", x2$q95, " mm)")
x2.mean.full <- paste0("(mean = ", x2$Mean, " mm, 5th percentile = ", x2$q05, " mm, 95th percentile = ", x2$q95, " mm)")

return(list(spp.out = x2$Species, range.alone = x2$range05.95, mean.alone = x2$Mean,
            spp.range = x2.range, 
            spp.range.full = x2.range.full, spp.mean.full = x2.mean.full
            ))
}

# Abstract

Western North American forests are experiencing accelerating tree mortality rates alongside intensifying drought and water stress.  Tree growth and mortality reflect cumulative effects of direct physiological stress (xylem cavitation, carbon starvation), and indirect climate-mediated impacts (wildfire, insects, pathogens).  Relating design-based estimates for mortality and growth to a climate variable can be challenging, as directly assessing mortality and growth requires the visitation of plots at two different points in time.  Plots can differ both in their initial climate variable value and the change in that value between visits, necessitating estimation domains that jointly consider initial conditions and temporal change. We developed an analysis framework that partitions plots into domains defined by their initial-visit climatic water deficit (CWD) value and the change in the CWD value between visits.  We applied this approach to `r comma(analysis.stats$plot.num)` National Forest Inventory (FIA) plots spanning California, Oregon, and Washington, tracking `r comma(analysis.stats$tree.num)` trees from `r n.spp` species over decade-long intervals.  We estimated decadal growth and mortality across three states, by state, and for six CWD domains per species, along with associated measures of uncertainty.  Species responses were highly variable, with no universal pattern of increased mortality or reduced growth in domains experiencing elevated water stress. Several species exhibited overall mortality rates exceeding 0.20 (i.e., 20% decadal mortality), with estimates of 0.35 for *Picea engelmannii* in Washington, 0.27 for *Acer macrophyllum* in California, and 0.37 for *Pinus contorta* in Washington. Domain-specific patterns aligned with known regional disturbances (bark beetles, drought, fire) for multiple species.  We found that CWD increased in 91.6% of plots. The FIA sampling design enabled our study to contribute reliable regional insights into the condition of several tree species that exhibit high mortality and low growth rates. 


# 1. Introduction

Western North American forests are experiencing increases in tree mortality across multiple species in concert with changing climate conditions.  Species and tree groups have incurred extraordinary losses in specific regions.  Johnston et al. [1] documented a 29% 10-year mortality rate of 300+ yr old trees in Eastern Oregon.  High-severity fires in California in 2020 and 2021 killed 13%-19% of extant giant sequoia (*Sequoiadendron giganteum*) with >1.07-m bole diameters [2,3]; recruitment in these burns was depressed [4].  Species and genera have also seen their mortality rates increase overall. For example, van Mantgem et al. [5] found modeled mortality rates for the genera *Abies* and *Pinus* in the western USA increased from less than 0.05% annually in 1960 to almost 0.2% by 2010. Perret et al. [6] estimated a decadal range-wide mortality rate of 25% for Subalpine fir (*Picea engelmannii*). Five of eight common tree species in western North America exhibit declines as measured by relative stand density [7].  Shriver et al. [8] found that four of five juniper (*Juniperus* spp.) and piñon pine (*Pinus* spp.) species were declining in portions of their range, comparing mortality to recruitment rates.      

Climate change manifested through increases or intensification in drought and aridity can affect tree mortality directly and indirectly.  Direct impacts include physiological damage while indirect causes include increasing wildfire, insect, and disease outbreak frequency and severity.  Hammond et al. [9] found globally that the intensity of drought and heat events are directly associated with widespread forest die-off events.  Wildfire frequency and area burned in the western United States has increased in concert with the longer fire seasons, hotter summer temperatures, and earlier snowmelt [10–12]. There have also been regional increases in the area affected by bark beetle outbreaks (subfamily *Scolytinae* spp.) [13,14].  Many of these indirect climate-influenced mortality causes may be attributable to the physical condition of trees following abnormal or prolonged exposure to water stress.   

Carbon starvation and hydraulic failure can drive drought-induced mortality (see reviews by [15–18]).  Carbon starvation occurs when isohydric species (e.g., piñon pine, *Pinus edulis* [19]), or those which mainly rely on stomatal closure to avoid excessive water loss through evapotranspiration (ET), receive insufficient atmospheric carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.  Anisohydric plants, or those that do not strongly regulate water loss through stomatal closure, risk hydraulic failure if sufficient xylem cavitation occurs due to insufficient water uptake needed to meet ET demands (e.g., *Populus tremuloides* [20]). Adams et al. [21] performed a review of drought-induced mortality across 26 species and concluded that hydraulic failure occurred broadly across taxa while non-structural carbohydrate reserves at the time of mortality differed across taxa.  Regardless of mechanism, drought (specifically, water deficit) appears to be an important direct driver of mortality for tree taxa [9].   

Given the importance of water stress on tree mortality, selecting an appropriate metric is critical for rangewide assessments.  One regionally useful metric of water stress is Climatic Water Deficit (CWD) [22].  Stephenson [23] defined CWD as evaporative demand not met by available water, or the difference between plant water demand (actual evapotranspiration, AET), and plant water supply (potential evapotranspiration); these variables are driven by temperature and precipitation, respectively.  Anderegg et al. [20] conducted a tree mortality study that relied on CWD to capture drought occurrence.  Das et al. [24] determined that low-elevation California tree mortality was best modeled using CWD.  Restaino et al. [25] found decreased Douglass fir growth with an increase in CWD.    

Data from the U.S. National Forest Inventory, collected by the US Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis Program (FIA), is well suited for evaluating regional species growth and mortality. Since 1999 the FIA program has gathered a variety of forestry data at plots nationwide using a spatially balanced sampling design [26–28].  The sampling design allows for approximately unbiased design-based inference of population characteristics across large geographical regions and is especially well suited for quantifying large scale climatic effects on populations of trees.  Data from plot revisits permit robust estimation of change features such as mortality and growth rates   

Climatic data such as mean annual temperature and CWD can be combined with FIA data to obtain climate-related design-based estimates. Monleon and Lintz [29] evaluated the evidence of tree species range shifts by subtracting the design-based mean estimates of FIA plot temperatures for seedlings from those of mature trees. However, FIA plot revisit data were mostly incomplete at the time of their analysis. In contrast, Groom and Monleon [30] used nearly completed revisit data to compare plot climate variable values (vapor pressure deficit [VPD], temperature, and precipitation) to estimate shifts in plot occupancy and density.  Both studies used a single climate variable value associated with each plot for estimation; e.g., Groom and Monleon [30] examined shifts in species density by estimating the difference in VPD means between plots that gained trees of a given species and plots that lost trees. They documented that the initial values of a climate variable could (and often did) change between plot visits, with species' plots exhibiting positive or negative correlations between the values of the climate variable at the initial visit and changes in the values at subsequent visits. They identified that their design-based analysis would potentially improve if they could simultaneously include both initial visit and change values for the climate variable.   

Our study has two objectives.  The first is to utilize a design-based estimation approach for tree growth and mortality across 23 species that simultaneously accounts for initial plot CWD values and the change in CWD values between measurements. The approach relies on domain estimation, where domains are defined by initial plot conditions and the change in those conditions between visits. The analysis evaluates differences in domains by estimating contrasts among them.  Second, we provide current growth and mortality estimates for our analysis species across our study area and by state to establish species status and to inform our climate analysis findings.  



# 2. Methods  

## 2.1 FIA data  

Our analysis relies on FIA data for forestland in California, Oregon, and Washington, USA.  Forestland is defined as an area of at least 4,050 m^2^ (i.e., one acre) that is at least 10 percent stocked or potentially stocked with tree species, excluding urban and agricultural land uses [27].  We constrained our analysis to only include remeasurements for areas considered forestland during both visits.  

In the coterminous United States the FIA program uses a spatially balanced, quasi-systematic sampling design. Plots are randomly located and produce sampling intensities of approximately 2,400 hectares per plot, with some denser areas such as those located on national forest system lands. In the western United States, each plot is assigned to one of ten panels, and approximately one panel is measured each year in perpetuity, yielding ten-year remeasurement intervals on each plot, barring exceptions owing to optional temporal intensifications [31]. In this study, we use only those plots that are part of the standard sampling intensity. Each FIA plot consists, in part, of four 7.32 m radius subplots where all trees with stem diameters greater than or equal to 12.7 cm (for most species measured at 1.37 m above the ground) were tallied with additional trees sampled in an annulus around each subplot (macroplot), with a total radius 18 m from the center point and a total area of 1012 m^2^.  We did not include data from microplots, where seedlings and saplings are measured, as the analysis was not intended to estimate species recruitment but rather to follow the trajectory of established trees. Reams et al. [27] and Bechtold and Scott [32] provide plot design details and measurement protocols.   

Our analysis examines the growth and mortality of individual trees measured during two sequential visits (referred to as the first and second plot visit), from a sample containing complete remeasurements. Tree growth is the observed increase in marked tree bole area between visits (cm^2^) while mortality is captured from the change in tree condition. The calculation for tree growth, basal area increment (BAI) on a decadal time scale, is calculated as   

$$BAI=\pi R_{t2}^2\ -\ \pi R_{t1}^2\ \ $$
where $R$ is the bole radius at times 1 and 2.  Annual changes in tree diameter [33] and basal area [34] can vary greatly among trees and over time. Annual BAI for a species overall can increase disproportionately over time (e.g., [35]) while annual diameter increment can decrease (e.g., [36]) even with an increase in BAI. Due to the potential influence of different initial diameters on BAI, we include growth estimates for differences in tree diameter between t2 and t1 in the Supplemental Materials (S2 Table and S1 Figure).     

We obtained our FIA data from the USDA FIA DataMart web portal (https://research.fs.usda.gov/products/dataandtools/fia-datamart; downloaded May 5, 2025).  The database included plot data sampled from 2001 to 2023. We limited the number of species examined to those with more than 400 occupied plots across the states of Oregon, Washington, and California.    


## 2.2 Climate data and species classification

We obtained plot-level CWD data from the TerraClimate dataset [37] for June, July, and August (summer months) between 1980 and 2023. In general, access to true plot coordinates is restricted to internal FIA staff or those approved to view them. For general use, FIA makes a set of perturbed  plot coordinates available to the public, which are randomized locations typically located within 1.6 km of the true position, and up to 20 percent of plots on private land swapped with other randomized locations in similar forest types [38].  Perturbed plot coordinates have the potential to weaken correlations between forest attributes of interest and spatially explicit climate covariates, like the CWD data used in this study, because the perturbed locations may land in areas experiencing different climatic conditions. We determined that the Pearson's correlation between the public and confidential CWD plot values was > 0.99, so for simplicity we used the CWD values derived from public coordinates. The second author is authorized to handle confidential coordinates and conducted the correlation analysis. Using the public coordinates facilitates scientific replication by those external to FIA, and they are available in the database used for this study. We defined 'initial CWD' values as the 20-year mean of summer CWD values for each plot prior to and including the first visit year (initial CWD = mean of summer CWD from visit year$_{-19}$ to year$_0$).  We then found the mean of summer CWD values between visits and including the second visit year (second visit CWD = mean of summer CWD from year$_1$ to year$_10$).  We then defined 'delta CWD' as the second visit CWD values minus initial CWD values.  Figure `r fig_nums("fig_cwdmap", display = "num")` presents maps of both the initial CWD and delta CWD values for forested and nonforested FIA plots.  

We coarsely categorized tree species by several taxonomic and ecological characteristics, such as tree type (angiosperm [hardwood] vs. conifer), drought tolerance, fire adaption, elevation, shade tolerance, and mesic and riparian specialization.  We obtained the category information from https://plants.usda.gov/ (accessed 12/12/2025) and Burns and Honkala [39,40].  Categorization was done to aid the presentation of results; some species could fall under more than one category (e.g., we classified *Picea engelmannii* as a high elevation conifer [HEC] while it could have been classified as a shade-tolerant conifer [STC]).  Our categories with abbreviations also include fire-adapted conifers (FAC), drought-tolerant conifers (DTC), drought-tolerant hardwoods (DTH) and riparian and mesic hardwoods (RMH).  These abbreviations are used in Tables `r tab_nums("tbl_growth", display = "num")` and `r tab_nums("tbl_mort", display = "num")`. 

## 2.3 Analysis and dashboard
We obtained point estimates of growth and mortality using standard FIA estimators from Scott et al. [41]. In this study, both growth and mortality can be framed as ratios, which manifest as special cases of the ratio estimator presented in Scott et al. For the case of growth, we develop an estimator for the growth rate of domain $d$ as 

$$\hat{G}_d = \frac{\hat{Y}_d}{\hat{S}_d}$$

where ${\hat{S}}_d$ is an estimator for the stem density of survivor trees (i.e., those trees that were alive at both visits) and ${\hat{Y}}_d$ is an estimator for the total basal area growth occurring over a decade ($\Delta$ cm^2^ ha^-1^) for those trees, yielding a decadal survivor growth rate on an individual tree basis. The domain index, $d$, is used to differentiate estimators of different granularity, e.g., to refer to estimators for particular species and within particular climatic water deficit envelopes, developed in later methods. The estimator for mortality is similar in structure:   

$${\hat{M}}_d=\frac{{\hat{D}}_d}{{\hat{L}}_d}$$

where ${\hat{L}}_d$ is an estimator of the live stem density at the initial visit, and ${\hat{D}}_d$ is an estimator of stem density of trees that died between visits and were alive at the initial visit. Due to the 10-year remeasurement interval, ${\hat{M}}_d$ yields a decadal mortality rate, which is commonly reported in studies that use FIA data (e.g., [6]). The four individual estimators, ${\hat{Y}}_d$, ${\hat{S}}_d$, ${\hat{D}}_d$, and ${\hat{L}}_d$ are post-stratified estimators, a standard FIA estimation technique, which is made by estimating post-stratum means and aggregating to the estimates of totals, given above (see S1 Appendix).    

The simplicity of the above estimators conceals a layer of complexity involved with which trees are included in each estimate, and requires further specification. For the growth estimator trees are included if they are at least 12.7 cm in diameter and alive at both visits. For the mortality estimator trees are included if they are at least 12.7 cm in diameter and alive at the initial visit, and trees killed by silvicultural practices are not included. Both estimators do not include trees that shrank in diameter, physically moved due to landslides or other events, were erroneously tallied at either visit, were missed due to data collection procedural changes, or were located in a nonsampled area at either visit.   

We estimate species’ overall, state (Washington, Oregon, and California), and climatic domain means and measures of uncertainty for both mortality and growth. We use six climatic domains based on CWD values, IL, IM, IH, SL, SM, and SH (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_domains", display = "num")`C). The domain designations IL, IM, and IH correspond to the classifications of Increasing Low, Increasing Medium, and Increasing High. The Stable domains are designated similarly.  The Low, Medium and High aspects of the domain classification refer to a partitioning of initial CWD values into three species-specific quantiles: values below the first quartile (Low), between the first and third quartiles (Medium), and above the third quartile (High). We defined the Increasing and Stable components as delta CWD values for all species that fell respectively above or below a 5 mm CWD change threshold. We applied the 5 mm threshold across species because species’ delta CWD value distributions did not differ greatly and because 5 mm is approximately the grand mean delta CWD value (S3 Table). The Stable domains may include some negative delta CWD values (i.e., the mean CWD value was larger prior to the initial visit than between visits); however, these instances were rare and of small magnitude. These six within-domain estimates allowed us to establish mortality and growth rates for trees of a given species that experienced similar climatic conditions (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_domains", display = "num")`A and B). We calculated growth and mortality estimates for each domain with 10 or more plots.  

In addition to within-domain estimates, we examined growth and mortality contrasts among CWD domains. This allowed us to evaluate if trees between two CWD domains are experiencing meaningful differences in growth and mortality. For example, estimates of contrasts reveal whether trees in historically dry sites (High initial CWD) respond differently to increased water stress (Increasing, or above threshold delta CWD) compared to trees in mesic sites (Low initial CWD) experiencing similar increases, among other comparisons.  

We obtained empirical means and 95% confidence intervals via a nonparametric bootstrap to allow for asymmetrical CIs around means. For each of the 1000 bootstrap iterations we sampled FIA plots with replacement and obtained species point estimates for each domain, yielding a maximum of `r n.spp * 6 ` CWD domain point estimates for each iteration.  For each domain we calculated a mean, upper, and lower 95% CI with the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles from the  bootstrap iterations.  We estimated contrasts between pairs of CWD domains by subtracting within-iteration domain point estimates.   

Our contrast analysis approach resulted in hundreds of comparisons. Given the large number of tests, we encourage readers to interpret significant differences (i.e., contrast 95% CIs that do not include zero) with caution, as some proportion likely represent Type-I errors and occurred by chance.  We did not apply a multiple comparisons correction as (1) our analysis is inherently exploratory, aimed at identifying patterns within and across species rather than testing a specific *a priori* hypothesis, and (2) because we did not want to inflate the Type-II error rate and obscure real relationships in favor of reducing false positive findings.   

We developed a data dashboard (https://tinyurl.com/FIAgrowmort) to enable ourselves and readers to examine individual species domain estimates for growth and mortality, the distribution of initial and delta CWD values, and the public geographic locations of plots, plot domains, and mortality causes on plots.  All analysis files, manuscript markdowns, dashboard code, and ancillary data sources are available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/jeremygroom/Tree_Growth_Death.  


# 3. Results

Our study tracked the fate of `r comma(analysis.stats$tree.num)` trees from `r n.spp` species in `r comma(analysis.stats$plot.num)` plots that were visited twice by FIA crews. Of the `r n.spp` species, `r analysis.stats$n.gym.spp` were gymnosperms.  The two visits were 10 years apart for `r pct.remeas[2]`% of plots (`r pct.remeas[1]`% were 9 years and `r pct.remeas[3]`% were 11 years apart). Plots were distributed across `r analysis.stats$strat.num` strata spanning forested regions in all three states, from coastal temperate rainforest to semi-arid interior woodlands.  

## 3.1 Climatic Water Deficit

Delta CWD was greater than zero (i.e., CWD increased) for `r analysis.stats$cwd.gt0.pct`% of plots. The increases occurred in all forested regions of the three states (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_cwdmap", display = "num")`C).  Plots where CWD decreased (indicated by negative delta CWD values) are presented alone in S2 Figure.  For Washington and Oregon, negative CWD values were almost entirely found in the Coast Ranges and the mesic west slope of the Cascades Range crest.  The Blue Mountains and northern and northeastern Washington lacked negative delta CWD plots entirely. In California negative delta CWD plots with values < -1.0 mm were primarily found in the northern Sierra Nevada and in the southern portions of the state. Overall, there was a weak, positive linear correlation (Pearson's correlation = `r CWD.lin.cor`) between initial and delta CWD values. The two variables were better modeled with a 3rd order polynomial although the resulting R^2^ value still indicated that the variance was not well explained by the model ($\Delta AIC$ =  `r CWD.dAIC`, R^2^ = `r round(CWD.rels$lm2$r.squared, 2)`, S3 Figure, S4 and S5 Tables), implying that other processes likely affected the relationship between initial and delta CWD. For most species delta CWD neither linearly related to nor monotonically increased with initial CWD values (S4 Figure; see dashboard). For instance, the relationship between the initial and delta CWD values for *Calocedrus decurrens* may be described overall with a concave curve, with some of the most negative delta CWD values occurring in the High domain (along with some of largest delta CWD values; Figure `r fig_nums("fig_domains", display = "num")`C).  

The distribution of initial CWD values across the three states (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_cwdmap", display = "num")`A) reflected total annual precipitation normals for 1991-2000 (check against https://www.climate.gov/media/13728).  The most mesic areas, the Coast Ranges and the west slope of the Cascade Range, coincided with the areas with the lowest initial CWD values.   

Initial CWD means and ranges differed among tree species (S6 Table).  The `r n.spp` species appeared to form two different groups by initial CWD and delta CWD (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_cwdmeans", display = "num")`).  Eight species had mean delta CWD values < 4.5 mm and mean initial CWD values < 100 mm, and were well represented in the mesic Coast Ranges, coastal northwestern California, and the western slope of the Cascade Range (dashboard).  *`r init.mean.sm$spp.out`* had the smallest mean value for initial CWD (`r init.mean.sm$mean.alone` mm) while *`r init.range.sm$spp.out`* had both the largest mean value (`r init.mean.lg$mean.alone` mm) and smallest range `r init.range.sm$spp.range`.  *`r init.range.lg$spp.out`* occupied the plots with the largest range of initial CWD values `r init.range.lg$spp.range` and was the most widely distributed of the 23 species examined (dashboard). Aside from drought-tolerant conifers and riparian and mesic hardwoods our ecological categorization of the species were not captured within one of these two initial and delta CWD groups.    

Species did not differ greatly by delta CWD (S3 Table).   The riparian species *`r delta.mean.sm$spp.out`* had the smallest mean delta CWD value of `r delta.mean.sm$mean.alone` mm `r delta.mean.sm$spp.range`.  The species with the second smallest mean (`r delta.mean.sm2$mean.alone`mm) and smallest range of delta CWD values `r delta.mean.sm2$spp.range` was the largely coastal *`r delta.mean.sm2$spp.out`*.  The mostly high-elevation *`r delta.mean.lg$spp.out`* had the largest mean increase in CWD values of `r delta.mean.lg$mean.alone` mm `r delta.mean.lg$spp.range`.  *`r delta.range.lg$spp.out`*, another high-elevation species, had the greatest range in delta CWD values `r delta.range.lg$spp.range`.   

## 3.2 Growth

Patterns of state growth rates by decadal BAI (presented) generally aligned with diameter increment (S2 Table).  Overall growth rates differed by species but in some instances coincided with species’ ecological traits.  For instance, the drought-tolerant hardwoods (*Arbutus menziesii*, *Notholithocarpus densiflorus*, *Quercus chrysolepis*, and *Quercus kelloggii*) exhibited the lowest growth rates overall (< 75 cm^2^ / decade, Table 1).  Riparian and mesic hardwoods like *Acer macrophyllum* and *Alnus rubra* on average grew by 145 cm^2^/decade, although growth for *Acer macrophyllum* varied by state; its mean growth in California was 52.3 cm^2^/decade, less than half of its growth rate in Oregon and almost four times less than its growth rate in Washington.  There was variation in high-elevation conifer growth;  *Abies concolor* and *Picea engelmannii* grew at similar rates in Oregon, approximately 170-190 cm^2^/decade, while in Washington *Picea engelmannii* grew at only 125.4 cm^2^/decade. The other high-elevation conifers, *Abies lasiocarpa*, and *Tsuga mertensiana* grew more slowly at almost 70 cm^2^/decade.   

Shade tolerant conifers (*Abies amabilis*, *Abies grandis*, *Pinus lambertiana*, *Thuja plicata*, and *Tsuga heterophylla*) grew at moderate (109.9 cm^2^/decade for *Abies amabilis*) to high rates (*Pinus lambertiana* had the highest overall growth rate of 253.6 cm^2^/decade). The fire-adapted conifers exhibited a range of mean growth rates, with *Pseudotsuga menziesii* having the greatest mean growth rate (229.9 cm^2^/decade), *Pinus monticola* and *Larix occidentalis* exhibiting moderate growth (124.8 and 106.4 cm^2^/decade, respectively), and *Pinus contorta* with the lowest mean growth rate (69.3 cm^2^/decade). The confidence intervals for *Pinus contorta* growth rates did not overlap between California and either Oregon or Washington; growth rates were highest in California (83.8 cm^2^/decade) and lowest in Washington (57.0 cm^2^/decade).  Conversely *Pinus monticola* had a mean growth rate in Washington of 172.4 cm^2^/decade and lower growth rates in Oregon and California (approximately 116 cm^2^/decade for both).  The mean growth rates for three drought-tolerant conifers (*Calocedrus decurrens*, *Pinus jeffreyi*, and *Pinus ponderosa*) were above 140 cm^2^/decade while the growth rate for *Juniperus occidentalis* was approximately half of that value, at 68.7 cm^2^/decade.    

`r t.ref("tbl_summ_grow_mort")` summarizes the number of domain differences in each of the columns in Figures `r fig_nums("fig_diffgrow", display = "num")` and `r fig_nums("fig_diffmort", display = "num")` where the 95% CI does not include zero as well as the number of contrasts per figure column. Growth domain contrasts (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_diffgrow", display = "num")`, `r t.ref("tbl_summ_grow_mort")`) did not appear to result in substantially more significant  negative or positive estimates, indicating that species overall did not exhibit higher or lower growth rates in the Increasing, Low, or High domains. The figure column “Increasing vs. Stable” displays the mean point estimate and 95% CI for contrasts between the Increasing and Stable domains (e.g., for *Abies lasiocarpa*, subtracting the estimates for columns SL, SM, and SH from IL, IM, IH, respectively; Figure `r fig_nums("fig_domains", display = "num")`A). Negative estimates in the “Increasing vs. Stable” columns in Figures `r fig_nums("fig_diffgrow", display = "num")` and `r fig_nums("fig_diffmort", display = "num")` indicate that the 10-year growth or mortality rate was higher for a species in Stable domains.    

We observed varying growth rates across the CWD domains (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_diffgrow", display = "num")`, similar patterns reflected for diameter increment in S1 Figure). The patterns of CWD domain estimates for growth were not necessarily reflected in mortality estimates (e.g., Figures `r fig_nums("fig_domains", display = "num")`A and `r fig_nums("fig_domains", display = "num")`B). Depending on the species, growth may have been associated (negatively or positively) to a change in CWD and/or differed by initial CWD values. *Abies amabilis*, *Abies grandis*, *Calocedrus decurrens*, *Pinus ponderosa*, *Pseudotsuga menziesii*, *Tsuga mertensiana*, *Acer macrophyllum*, and *Alnus rubra* exhibited greater growth in the Low (less initial water stress) domains than the Medium and/or High domains. This was exemplified by *Acer macrophyllum* and *Abies grandis* with a mean difference of `r fig.val.fcn("g", "X312", "IH - IL", 0)` cm^2^/decade, IH-IL and `r fig.val.fcn("g", "X312", "SH - SL", 0)` cm^2^/decade, SH-SL. *Thuja plicata* had higher growth rates in the Medium domains than either High or Low domains (Increasing: `r fig.val.fcn("g", "X242", "IH - IM", 0)` cm^2^/decade for IH-IM and `r fig.val.fcn("g", "X242", "IM - IL", 0)` cm^2^/decade for IM-IL; Stable: `r fig.val.fcn("g", "X242", "SH - SM", 0)` cm^2^/decade for SH-SM and `r fig.val.fcn("g", "X242", "SM - SL", 0)` cm^2^/decade for SM-SL). *Abies concolor*, *Larix occidentalis*, *Picea engelmannii*, *Pinus contorta*, *Pinus lambertiana*, *Arbutus menziesii*, and *Quercus kelloggii* had higher growth rates in the more water stressed High domains than the Medium and/or Low domains, with some of the greatest differences for *Pinus lambertiana* (`r fig.val.fcn("g", "X117", "IH - IL", 0)` cm^2^/decade for IH-IL) and *Picea engelmannii* (`r fig.val.fcn("g", "X93", "SH - SL", 0)` cm^2^/decade for SH-SL).    


## 3.3 Mortality  

Overall decadal mean mortality rates were highest among high elevation conifers. Three out of the four species had mortality rates of 0.20/decade or higher, including *Picea engelmannii* with the highest mean mortality rate of 0.28/decade (95% CI = 0.21, 0.36).  This species exhibited a mean mortality rate that was almost five times higher in Washington (0.34) than in Oregon (0.07).  Drought-tolerant conifers had overall mortality rates that were relatively low (*Calocedrus decurrens* had the greatest mortality of the four species at 0.15/decade). *Calocedrus decurrens* and *Pinus ponderosa* both exhibited higher mortality and lower growth rates in California than Oregon. The mean mortality rates for drought-tolerant hardwoods ranged from 0.14 to 0.20, with *Quercus chrysolepis* and *Quercus kelloggii* having the highest mortality rates (0.20 and 0.18, respectively).  Of the fire-adapted conifers, *Pinus monticola* and *Pinus contorta* had the greatest mortality rates (0.19 and 0.20, respectively), with *Pinus contorta* exhibiting a low decadal mortality rate in California (0.07), more than twice that rate in Oregon (0.17), and five times the California rate in Washington (0.37).  For the riparian and mesic hardwoods, *Alnus rubra* had an overall decadal mortality rate of 0.21, compared to 0.13 for *Acer macrophyllum*.  However, *Acer macrophyllum* exhibited a mortality rate of 0.27/decade in California, almost three times as high as Washington and Oregon. Decadal mortality rates for shade-tolerant conifers varied greatly, from 0.04 (*Thuja plicata*) to 0.20 (*Pinus lambertiana*).  The mortality rate for *Abies grandis* in Washington was approximately twice as high as the rates for Oregon and California.    

A suite of species had greater mortality in the Low domains than the Medium and/or High domains including *Larix occidentalis*, *Picea engelmannii*, *Pinus contorta*, *Pinus monticola*, and *Thuja plicata*. Some of the most negative mean mortality contrasts (Figure 5) included *Picea engelmannii* and *Pinus contorta* (`r fig.val.fcn("m", "X93", "IH - IL", 2)` and `r fig.val.fcn("m", "X108", "IH - IL", 2)`/decade, respectively, for IH-IL). Mortality rates for *Abies lasiocarpa*, *Calocedrus decurrens*, *Pinus lambertiana*, *Pinus ponderosa*, *Pseudotsuga menziesii*, *Tsuga heterophylla*, *Tsuga mertensiana*, *Acer macrophyllum*, and *Notholithocarpus densiflorus* were higher in the High domains than the Medium and/or Low domains.  The highest positive estimates include `r fig.val.fcn("m", "X19", "SH - SL", 2)`/decade for the *Abies lasiocarpa* SH-SL contrast, and `r fig.val.fcn("m", "X117", "IH - IM", 2)`/decade for the *Pinus lambertiana* IH-IM contrast.      

Like growth domain contrasts, the three types of mortality contrasts did not appear to be predominantly positive or negative (Figure `r fig_nums("fig_diffmort", display = "num")`, `r t.ref("tbl_summ_grow_mort")`). There were fewer mortality estimates with significant findings than growth (46 vs 74). There were fewer differences for “Increasing vs. Stable” contrasts (9) than for Increasing (21) or Stable (16), indicating that mortality may have been more weakly associated with delta CWD than initial CWD values.

## 3.4 Geography  
The interactive dashboard revealed geographic patterns that were associated with specific domains while not necessarily captured by state-level estimates. For the Increasing and Stable Low domains *Abies lasiocarpa* had less mortality in northeastern Washington and *Tsuga mertensiana* exhibited greater growth in the same region. *Pinus contorta* exhibited less growth and greater mortality in northern Washington (Increasing Low). In the southern Sierra Nevada *Pinus lambertiana* had greater growth (Increasing Medium and High) and greater mortality (Increasing High), *Calocedrus decurrens* had greater mortality (Increasing High), and *Pinus monticola* had less mortality (Increasing High). *Acer macrophyllum* exhibited less growth in the Sierra Nevada and southern Klamath Mountains (Increasing High) and greater growth in northwestern Washington in the Coast and Cascade ranges (Increasing and Stable Low).



# 4. Discussion

Analysis of 23 tree species revealed species-level regional differences in growth and mortality rates as well as differences in rates by ecological groups.  We found that CWD increased in over 90% of plots over the 10 years between visits, the increase in delta CWD was generally not large relative to initial CWD values, all-plot delta CWD values were not linearly related to initial CWD values, and the relationship between the two metrics was not consistent across individual species plots. The species-specific CWD domain analysis revealed diverse associations with climatic water deficit, with different species exhibiting contrasting relationships among growth, mortality, and water stress. We found more significant CWD contrasts for species growth than mortality, possibly indicating that growth differences by CWD domain were more readily detectable than mortality over a decade, although growth and mortality findings were not necessarily negatively related. We did not detect patterns among species’ CWD domain contrasts which we interpret as a negative finding: species responses among CWD domains did not appear generalizable and were potentially driven by differences in drought tolerance strategies, local disturbance regimes, and biotic interactions.    

This analysis provided a large scale (3 state) and broad (23 species) examination of mortality and growth signals.  Most demographic analyses of tree species, particularly those using FIA data, focus on one [6,42] or fewer than ten [7,8,43–45] species, with exceptions (e.g., [29,30,46]).  Examining fewer, especially more numerous tree species would permit greater analysis depth than we could achieve here. Our analysis instead allows for the identification of subpopulations of tree species, by state or CWD domain, that exhibit high or low growth or mortality rates.  Although the contrast analyses did not reveal systematic patterns of differences among CWD domains, it did provide species-specific differences in growth and mortality, some of which reflected localized subpopulation conditions.        

The availability of a complete set of FIA revisit data in the states we investigated is a relatively recent development. Prior to the availability of the revisit data, Monleon and Lintz [29] assessed tree species’ range shifts using the single-visit data set, comparing mean plot temperature values for sapling and mature trees. Groom and Monleon [30] accessed a partial FIA revisit data set and found evidence of tree species density shifts along initial values of climatic variables but documented evidence of interactions between those variables’ initial and change values. The current examination approach for initial and delta CWD plot values shares some dimensional similarities with Dobrowski et al. [47] who examined the velocity of CWD (change in distance over time) along with AET and minimum temperatures. Our CWD domain approach allowed us to capitalize on the amenability of the data to design-based estimation while accounting for the need, when examining revisit conditions, of capturing the initial and change value conditions.    

## 4.1 Growth and Mortality

Our regional and state-level analyses detected several species with relatively high mortality rates (> 20%/decade) including *Acer macrophyllum*, *Picea engelmannii*, *Abies lasiocarpa*, *Pinus contorta*, and *Alnus rubra*. Our results for *Alnus rubra*, a species with a short lifespan, aligns with reported background mortality rates (e.g., [48]). Species growth rates by state roughly aligned with ecological groupings and frequently but not always mirrored mortality rates (e.g., *Calocedrus decurrens*).     

We estimated that the *Acer macrophyllum* growth rate was lower and mortality rate almost three times higher in California than in Washington and Oregon. These mortality rates are higher than the 0.45% annual mortality rate reported by McNellis et al. [46] for the three states, although their estimates excluded fire mortality (20% of this study’s *Acer macrophyllum* mortality was attributed to fire, unpublished data). Betzen et al. [49] found widespread evidence in Washington of *Acer macrophyllum* decline (crown dieback, thinning, discoloration, reduced leaf size) and reduced growth and increased mortality in locations with higher temperatures and water limitations.   

The high-elevation conspecific and frequently codominant species, *Abies lasiocarpa* and *Picea engelmannii*, exhibited high mortality rates. Mortality estimates for *Abies lasiocarpa* from Perret et al. [6] were similar to our state and overall estimates at 25% +/-2.7 per decade. They attributed 83% of the mortality to fire or biogenic disturbance and found harvested effects to be minor.      

The lower growth and higher mortality rate estimates for *Pinus contorta* in Washington may have reflected insect pressures on the species (also, see dashboard). The domains with the highest mortality and lowest growth align well with Washington regions that have experienced water stress [50]. Pine bark beetles (*Dendroctonus ponderosae*, *Dendroctonus brevicomis*, and *Ips* spp.) have affected *Pinus contorta* for the past decade in this region [51] (see dashboard).    

Our dashboard reveals some instances of domains that represent geographical differences in mortality. State estimates for *Pinus monticola* mortality do not appear to differ. Mortality for the Increasing High domain was low (see dashboard) and was predominantly represented by plots in the southern Sierra Nevada mountains of California. *Pinus lambertiana* and *Calocedrus decurrens* exhibited high mortality in approximately the same region, a result supported by Fettig et al. [52]. This region experienced an extreme drought that killed, as estimated from aerial detection surveys, 170 million trees between 2010 and 2021 [53]. Dudney et al. [54] also estimated lower mortality rates for *Pinus monticola* than for *Pinus lambertiana* in the Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks, which are within this region. They attributed some of the difference in mortality to elevation, with mountain pine beetle (*Dendroctonus ponderosae*), fire, and white pine blister rust (*Cronartium ribicola*) more prevalent at lower elevations, corresponding to the range of *Pinus lambertiana*.        


## 4.2 Climatic Water Deficit Findings and Issues  

Although CWD increased across most plots, the increase was not consistently nor linearly related to initial plot CWD values. This finding may be informative, as it implies that water stress may appear in portions of species ranges that have not historically been stressed, and that these patterns may differ by species.  At the broader scale of mean initial and delta CWD values, we did find some separation between trees with lower initial and delta CWD values from trees with higher initial CWD values. Species within our ecological categories generally crossed this separation; the two exceptions were the riparian and mesic hardwood species and drought-tolerant conifers. We believe this indicates that our ecological category classifications, in the context of CWD, are relatively uninformative.     

The absence of consistent contrast patterns across species may reflect interactions among species-specific patterns of initial and delta CWD values, physiology traits, adaption to local environments, and/or local events such as wildfire and insect and disease outbreaks (themselves potentially driven by CWD). The number of significant Increasing vs. Stable contrasts for growth and mortality were approximately evenly distributed between positive and negative contrasts, with a positive difference indicating that some species exhibited higher growth or greater mortality in an Increasing domain (e.g., *Pinus lambertiana* for both growth and mortality) versus a Stable domain (*Abies grandis* and *Pinus contorta*, respectively, for growth and mortality). This lack of a consistent pattern across species may indicate that the distinction of Increasing vs. Stable is not generalizable across species, or that significant findings are due to confounding factors such as geographical locations with different ecological pressures.    

CWD facilitates examining regional water stress as it integrates climatic and soil water availability through precipitation and air temperature data [22,23]. CWD correlates well with tree growth [25,55] and mortality [24,20,9]. However, there are some challenges in relying on CWD or any other climate variable in an extensive design-based analysis such as this one. The challenges stem from the remeasurement timeframe, using a fixed delta CWD domain threshold, the broad, fixed scope of our analysis, and the lack of incorporation of local-scale conditions.      

We did not detect sizable changes in CWD between visits, potentially signaling that 10 years is too soon to observe CWD-related species responses (perhaps truer for mortality than growth). Another possibility is that the spatial coarseness of the TerraClimate dataset (~4 km, [37]) potentially dampens the range of results we might see with a finer resolution climate model. The CWD changes we observed may have represented greater proportional change for some species than others, with species such as *Abies amabilis*, *Alnus rubra*, and *Juniperus occidentalis* exhibiting narrow initial CWD ranges.    

The broad scale of our study and the small number of variables we considered (two) likely limited our analysis because the evidence of water stress can manifest in multiple overlapping ways. Water stress alone can kill trees [20,56,57], but it can also increase the probability of insect [58–60] and wildfire-caused mortality [10]. With reference to Manion’s [61] “death spiral” (see also Bennett et al. [62] for a CWD-related version), teasing apart the cause of mortality from predisposing, inciting, and contributing factors is difficult at best, as these factors can interact [63]. Our regional analysis necessarily aggregates across local-scale variation in interrelated predisposing conditions for individual tree mortality such as canopy openness [64], structural complexity [65], possibly tree height [66,67], and within-stand competition [68]. For management applications, particularly those for individual stands, our regional and domain estimates should be viewed as general results that are likely impacted by these local factors.    

## 4.3 Future Refinements

Although our current analysis offers a coarse examination of species status across a large area, future analyses could refine our approach for assessing tree species growth and mortality by domains. Our climate domains could be divided further into sub-domains: trees could be assigned to categories by size, stand competition, plot aspect, or plot elevation within the climate domain categories. This approach has its limits: only estimates for certain widespread tree species would be reasonable to report, and domains could not be divided too finely into sub-domains due to sample size constraints, limiting the number of domain variables that could be considered simultaneously. However, this approach would likely permit design-based estimation at a resolution better attuned to capturing factors affecting growth and mortality.    

Our analysis captures significant changes in mortality and growth for the tree species we examined, with some trees exhibiting increases in mortality and decreases in growth either in portions of their ranges or across their entire range. For some species in semi-arid environments such as *Pinus ponderosa*, *Pseudotsuga menziesii*, *Pinus contorta*, *Picea engelmannii*, and *Abies lasiocarpa*, we may be observing ecosystem shifts with a change in water stress combined with disturbances such as wildfire and insect mortality [69,70,50].    



# 5. Conclusion

We assessed a mortality and growth rates for 23 species across the west coast of the United States. For the species examined we found no general patterns in CWD domains related to tree growth or mortality; rather, the results appeared species specific. Our analysis approach can be refined for individual species analysis, with the potential for integrating additional variables that could introduce information besides a condition variable and change variable. Results from our analysis and the analyses of others provide valuable and reliable insights into the condition of several tree species that exhibit high mortality and low growth. Our hope is that these findings will inform management and be of use in the development of monitoring efforts for these species in the rapidly changing landscape of western North America.

# Figure Captions
Figure 1: Public FIA plot locations displayed with values for initial visit CWD (A) and between-visit change in CWD (C) for the U.S. states, north to south, of Washington, Oregon, and California (see inset map B for the location of these states within the USA).  

Figure 2: Illustration of the domain analysis approach with *Calocedrus decurrens*. Columns A and B depict estimates for the six domain estimates (see text for definitions) for decadal growth and mortality, respectively.  C displays the distribution of plot initial and delta CWD values; the blue horizontal line demarcates the CWD change category threshold between Stable and Increasing, while orange vertical lines represent the quantile boundaries between Low, Medium, and High initial CWD values.  

Figure 3: Mean initial and change values for climatic water deficit for the 23 species examined, with coloration reflecting species ecological categories.   

Figure 4: Paired domain contrasts for mean growth rates (cm^2^ decade) by species.  Domain abbreviations are described in the text. See each column legend for the key of domain contrasts.  Mean domain contrasts (circles) with 95% CIs (bars) that do not intersect zero are filled. Species above the dashed line are conifers; those below are hardwoods.   

Figure 5. Paired domain contrasts for mean decadal mortality rates by species.  Domain abbreviations are described in the text. See each column legend for the key of domain contrasts.  Mean domain contrasts (circles) with 95% CIs (bars) that do not intersect zero are filled. Species above the dashed line are conifers; those below are hardwoods.
